paper_title: Seeing Is Locating: Spatial Awareness and Geographic Bias in Decision Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Language models are increasingly used for classification tasks such as labeling, grading, and routing. Decision models such as Jev (TypeSafe, 2026) and its open-weight counterparts (Palmer, 2026; Perplexity AI, 2026; Sthanika AI, 2026) are designed for this use: given an input and set of candidate labels, they output probability distribution over the labels instead of generating text, which makes them cheap, fast, and easy to deploy as classifiers and evaluators (Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026; Li 1 Figure 1: Top-1 predictions of pplx-decider-v1.2 on iNat2018 in the Image (top) and Image Location Prior (bottom) settings (Section 6.4). Green indicates correct predictions, and red indicates incorrect predictions. Figure design adapted from Wang et al. (2025a). et al., 2026). Many of these inputs involve real geographic locations, so fair decision model must leverage the spatial context of its input and minimize geographic bias at the same time. Geographic bias has been studied for generative LLMs (Manvi et al., 2024a) and for supervised geoaware models (Wu et al., 2024), whereas existing studies of decision models focus on how candidate labels are presented (Gao et al., 2026; Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026). The spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models therefore remain unexamined, even though they are increasingly used as zero-shot classifiers on geospatial tasks (Niu et al., 2026; Abouelhadid et al., 2026). We therefore ask three research questions: RQ1: Are decision models spatially aware? Can they predict from coordinates or place names, and do these inputs complement images? RQ2: Are decision models geographically biased? Are their errors spatially clustered and do their ratings of people and places correlate with socioeconomic conditions? RQ3: Can decision models be made spatially aware? Can spatial context be added to decision models without fine-tuning? To answer these questions, we introduce GEODECISIONS, multimodal benchmark with two tasks: ❶ geo-aware image classification, adapted from LocBench (Wu et al., 2024), and ❷ location rating, adapted from Manvi et al. (2024a). Evaluating six decision models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision (RQ1) and that decision models are geographically biased (RQ2). We then propose training-free method that combines decision models predictions with pretrained location prior, which improves spatial awareness (RQ3; Figure 1). Our contributions are threefold: GEODECISIONS benchmark. multimodal benchmark for decision models and shufflecorrected geo-bias scores that allow models with different accuracy to be compared. Systematic evaluation of spatial awareness and geographic bias. An evaluation of openweight and closed-source decision models, showing that spatial awareness requires vision, that decision models are geographically biased, and that this bias is largely inherited from base LLMs. Training-free spatial awareness. modelagnostic method that combines decision models with location prior to improve spatial awareness without substantially increasing geographic bias.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Geographic Bias in Language Models. LLMs encode substantial geographic knowledge: the coordinates of named places can be linearly decoded from their representations (Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024; Vafa et al., 2024), and socioeconomic indicators can be predicted from location prompts (Manvi et al., 2024b). Beyond social bias on attributes such as gender and race (Dhamala et al., 2021; Parrish et al., 2022), geography offers view of bias with measurable ground truth (Manvi et al., 2024a). LLMs recall geographic knowledge unevenly across countries (Moayeri et al., 2024), overamplify geopolitical favoritism (Faisal and Anastasopoulos, 2023), and rate locations with lower socioeconomic conditions lower on sensitive subjective topics (Manvi et al., 2024a). Likewise, vision and vision-language models (VLMs) are less accurate on images from lower-income regions (de Vries et al., 2019; Shankar et al., 2017; Nwatu et al., 2023). Urban-R1 (Wang et al., 2025a) mitigates such bias by fine-tuning VLMs with reinforcement learning via GRPO (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024). These studies target generative models, and mitigating bias through fine-tuning is computationally costly and requires access to model weights, which closed-source decision models such as Jev do not provide. We instead evaluate decision models and improve their spatial awareness with training-free method that applies to both open-weight and closed-source models (Section 5). Geo-Aware Benchmarks. Location encoders improve geo-aware tasks such as species recognition and remote sensing image classification (Mac Aodha et al., 2019; Mai et al., 2020, 2023, 2022) on fMoW (Christie et al., 2018), iNaturalist (Van Horn et al., 2018), and YFCC (Tang et al., 2015). TorchSpatial (Wu et al., 2024) unifies 15 location encoders in the LocBench benchmark and introduces geo-bias scores based on spatial selfinformation (Wang et al., 2024), later extended with spatial relative entropy in GeoBS (Wang et al., 2025b). These benchmarks show that location encoders increase geographic bias alongside accuracy, but evaluate only supervised models trained for each task. To our knowledge, no existing benchmark evaluates both the spatial awareness and geographic bias of (zero-shot) decision models, gap that GEODECISIONS fills by providing unified evaluation framework decision models. Decision Models. Decision (language) models output probability distribution over set of candidate labels instead of generating an answer or scoring answer tokens (Holtzman et al., 2021; Robinson and Wingate, 2023). Jev (TypeSafe, 2026) offers this as closed-source API, and several openweight models adapt Qwen and Gemma LLMs into decision models through fine-tuning (Palmer, 2026; Perplexity AI, 2026; Allahyar et al., 2026; PelaAI, 2026; Sthanika AI, 2026). Existing studies compare Jev with LLM judges (Rao and CallisonBurch, 2026; Li et al., 2026) and show that decision models underuse ordinal rating scales (Gao et al., 2026), echoing the label and position biases of LLMs (Zhao et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2024; Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024; Zheng et al., 2023; Stureborg et al., 2024). However, these studies only examine how labels are presented. Although decision models are increasingly used on geospatial tasks (Niu et al., 2026; Abouelhadid 2 et al., 2026), whether they are spatially aware or geographically biased remains understudied.

Following Wu et al. (2024) and Manvi et al. Task 2: location rating evaluates models ability to rate location on both objective and subjective topics given its coordinates, place name, or both,

sections.title: 4.2 Task 2: Location Rating
sections.content: Datasets. We adopt the 2,000 world locations released by Manvi et al. (2024a), which were sampled using their population-weighted importance sampling and farthest point sampling. Each location is rated on 6 objective topics (average temperature, annual precipitation, infant mortality rate, population density, nighttime light intensity, built-up area ratio), whose ground truth is aggregated from global rasters over 2525-pixel window around the location, following GeoLLM (Appendix C). Each location is also rated on 5 subjective topics without ground truth (average attractiveness, intelligence, likability, morality, work ethic of residents), on which an unbiased model gives constant or random rating at every location (Manvi et al., 2024a). Input Settings and Candidate Labels. Each location is evaluated under three input settings: ❶ Coordinates, where the model receives only the geographic coordinates; ❷ Place Name, where it receives only the address; and ❸ Full, where it receives the complete GeoLLM prompt, including coordinates, address, and nearby places (Manvi et al., 2024b). In all three settings, the model is asked to rate the location on given topic using the prompt from Manvi et al. (2024a) (Figure 2; Appendix B). The candidate labels are the 100 ratings from 0.0 to 9.9, and the prediction is the expected value of the rating under the models probability distribution over these labels (see Section 3).

sections.title: 4.3 Evaluation Metrics
sections.content: Accuracy. For Task 1, we report top-1 accuracy. For objective topics in Task 2, we report the Spearman rank correlation ρ between predicted ratings and ground truth (Manvi et al., 2024a). Shuffle-Corrected Geo-Bias Scores. To measure performance bias, we assign each sample performance value mi (its mark) at its location ℓi and test whether marks are spatially structured around set of evaluation centers, using the geobias scores of Wu et al. (2024) and Wang et al. (2025b). Briefly, SSI (spatial self-information) measures how unlikely the spatial autocorrelation of marks within each centers neighborhood is under random arrangement, and SRE (spatial relative entropy) divides each neighborhood into square cells and averages the KL divergence between the mark distribution of each cell and that of the neighborhood. Both scores, however, also depend on the overall mark distribution: model that is wrong almost everywhere obtains high SSI regardless of where its errors fall. We therefore subtract the score obtained after randomly permuting 4 the marks across samples, which preserves their distribution but removes their spatial structure: = S({(ℓi, mi)}N i=1) S({(ℓi, mπ(i))}N i=1), (2) where is SSI or SRE and π is fixed random permutation. SSI and SRE are zero in expectation when errors are spatially random, regardless of accuracy, and higher values indicate stronger clustering. We compute performance bias scores for Task 1 and use Hit@1 as the mark. Other evaluation metric parameters are provided in Appendix D. Social Bias Score. sections.title: Decision Models
sections.content: Despite encoding rich geographic knowledge about named places, multimodal language models struggle to leverage geographic coordinates as textual inputs, limitation also observed in decision models (Section 6.2). To address this limitation, we propose training-free method that combines decision models predictions with location prior from pretrained location encoder. Unlike generative LLMs, which produce free-form text, decision models output probability distributions over candidate labels, enabling direct probabilistic composition with an external location prior. We exploit this property to combine zero-shot decision model with pretrained location encoder, treating image and location as conditionally independent sources of evidence for the label. Formally, given sample with image I, location l, and candidate labels Y, we query the decision model using only the image and reweight its predictions with location prior g: p(y I, l) fθ(y I, Y) g(y l), (4) where g(y l) denotes the probability of observing label at location l, as estimated by the location encoder, and the product is normalized over Y. is evaluated only over the candidate labels and supports an arbitrary number of candidate labels K. It requires no parameter updates and uses only the decision models output probabilities, making it applicable to open-weight and closed-source models. Our method therefore represents location as distribution over candidate labels rather than as text prompts. Unlike existing supervised geo-aware models (Mac Aodha et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2024), our method uses zero-shot decision model without training on the target dataset. We apply this method to Task 1, where location provides spatial context for image classification, as fourth input setting ❹ Image Location Prior. We do not apply it to Task 2, as subjective ratings should be locationindependent, while prior over objective ratings would require training encoders on each groundtruth raster, which we leave to future work.

sections.title: 6.2 Spatial Awareness (RQ1)
sections.content: Table 2 reports top-1 accuracy on Task 1, and Table 3 reports Spearman ρ on Task 2 objective topics. Spatial awareness requires vision. Across the Task 1 datasets, the open-weight decision models perform poorly in the Coordinates setting, reaching at most 6.8% top-1 accuracy on YFCC, 4.4% on fMoW, 19.0% on iNat2017, and 18.5% on iNat2018. These results are only marginally above random guessing on YFCC and fMoW (1.0% and 1.6%), and below the Space2Vec-theory location prior alone on all four datasets. This suggests that coordinates alone give decision models insufficient spatial context for image classification, even though language models may implicitly encode spatial knowledge (Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024). In contrast, decision models perform significantly better in the Image setting compared to the Coordinates setting. On YFCC, which consists of everyday photos, the open-weight models reach 62.8 64.4% and outperform the supervised TorchSpatial image classifier (50.1%), but this advantage does not extend to the satellite (fMoW) and fine-grained species (iNat) images. In the Image + Coordinates setting, the open-weight models improve over the Image setting by 5.47.0% on the two iNat datasets, but gain negligibly on YFCC and fMoW. Human geography requires place names. On Task 2, the Coordinates setting allows decision models to rank locations by temperature, precipitation, and infant mortality (ρ = 0.690.88), but provides limited spatial context for nighttime lights, population density, and built-up ratio (ρ 0.40). In the Place Name setting, correlations on these 6 human-geography topics increase to ρ = 0.69 0.87. This gap likely reflects the spatial distribution of the topics: temperature, precipitation, and infant mortality vary smoothly across regions, whereas human geography is spatially heterogeneous at fine scales (e.g., urban vs. rural areas) and is tied to named places, which LLMs represent well (Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024). GPT-6 Luna is notable exception, reaching ρ 0.7 on human-geography topics even in the Coordinates setting. Decision fine-tuning brings modest gains. Comparing open-weight decision models with their base LLMs reveals that adapting LLMs into decision models yields modest gains in spatial awareness. On Task 1, decision fine-tuning brings marginal improvements in the Image setting, while in the Coordinates setting, only the Qwen-based models consistently outperform their base LLM. On Task 2, it improves rank correlations for temperature, precipitation, and infant mortality in the Coordinates setting, but has minimal impact in the Place Name and Full settings. Overall, decision fine-tuning mainly improves how models leverage coordinates as textual inputs, while most of their spatial knowledge comes from pretraining.

sections.title: 6.3 Geographic Bias (RQ2)
sections.content: Table 4 reports the shuffle-corrected geo-bias scores on Task 1, and Table 5 reports the bias scores on the subjective topics of Task 2. Decision models exhibit spatially clustered errors. On YFCC, decision models outperform TorchSpatial image classifiers in terms of accuracy, but their errors are 35 more spatially clustered in the Image setting (SSI 19.528.2 vs. 5.9), potentially reflecting regional imbalances in web pretraining data (de Vries et al., 2019). On iNat2017, adding Coordinates to the Image lowers SSI for all open-weight decision models (e.g., GLiDE-27B: 20.213.4), unlike TorchSpatial models whose errors become more spatially clustered when location prior is added (Wu et al., 2024). Geo-bias scores must be read together with accuracy; in the Coordinates setting, the decision models are only marginally above random guessing on YFCC and fMoW (Section 6.2), so most predictions are errors and their geo-bias scores are uninformative. On iNat, where accuracy in the Coordinates setting is substantially higher, Qwen-based decision models exhibit strongly clustered errors (SSI 69.393.2), indicating strong geographic performance bias. Decision models exhibit social bias. On all five subjective topics and in every input setting, all decision models give lower ratings in regions with lower socioeconomic conditions (B < 0). In the Full setting, intelligence is the most biased topic for every model except GPT-6 Luna. On intelligence, every model (except GPT-6 Luna) is more biased than GPT-3.5 Turbo. KnowLine-31B-Gen1, Sieve-31B-v3, and Jev-1.14 are also more biased than Gemini Pro, the most biased generative LLM reported by Manvi et al. (2024a) (Appendix D). This bias is largely inherited from the base LLMs, although decision fine-tuning may add bias on some topics. For instance, the base Gemma-4-31B-it is nearly unbiased on attractiveness and morality, whereas both Gemma-based decision models exhibit stronger bias on these topics. GPT-6 Luna is an exception: its is near zero on intelligence, attractiveness, and morality because it rates almost every location about 5.0 on these topics, yet its intelligence ratings remain correlated with infant mortality, and it refuses to answer 8.8% of intelligence questions, whereas Jev-1.14 refuses none. near-zero can thus hide biased ranking and should be read together with its correlation with socioeconomic conditions.

sections.title: 6.4 Spatial Awareness with a Location Prior

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: Location priors do not substantially increase geo-bias. Unlike the supervised TorchSpatial image classifier, whose errors on iNat become more spatially clustered with location prior (Wu et al., 2024), adding location prior does not substantially increase the spatial clustering of errors in the open-weight decision models. On iNat2018, the location prior substantially reduces SSI for all four open-weight decision models (34.253.9 6.3 7.3) and both base LLMs (37.248.9 4.98.7), well below the supervised baseline with the same prior. On iNat2017, SSI changes by at most +0.1 over the Image setting and stays below 18, whereas the supervised baseline rises from 40.1 to 53.9. SRE rises only slightly from .002.003 to .004 .005. Similarly, on fMoW, the location prior lowers SRE for all four open-weight decision models, in contrast to the increase observed for the supervised baseline. Adding location prior therefore improves the spatial awareness of decision models without the substantial increase in performance We introduced GEODECISIONS, multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. Across six decision models, we found that spatial awareness requires visual context, and that textual coordinates alone are insufficient for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. For location rating, coordinates allow decision models to rank locations by temperature, precipitation, and infant mortality, but place names are needed to capture human geography. We also found that decision models exhibit substantial geographic bias: the errors of open-weight decision models on everyday photos are more spatially clustered than those of supervised models, despite higher accuracy, and all six models give lower ratings to locations in regions with lower socioeconomic conditions. This bias is largely inherited from the base LLMs, but decision fine-tuning can further increase bias on some topics. Finally, our training-free method, which combines decision models with pretrained location prior, 8 improves spatial awareness without substantially increasing the performance bias of decision models. We release GEODECISIONS and our code to support future research on spatially aware and geographically fair decision models.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Evaluation Setup. Following Manvi et al. (2024a), we use infant mortality as the only proxy for socioeconomic conditions. Other proxies, such as population density, may capture different forms of social bias. Furthermore, our location prior uses TorchSpatial location encoders trained on each LocBench training split, making the prior datasetspecific. We therefore apply it only to Task 1 and leave its extension to Task 2 for future work. Comparability across Models. Image preprocessing varies across models: each openweight model uses its own image processor, while KnowLine-31B-Gen1 receives images resized to fit Jev-1.14s input size limits. Consequently, approximately 50% of fMoW images and 4% of YFCC images are upsampled for KnowLine-31B-Gen1. We also evaluate KnowLine-31B-Gen1 and Sieve-31B-v3 using their released inference configurations, which differ from those of other models by design. These include repeated prompting and task-specific temperatures for KnowLine-31B-Gen1, and two label orders and category-specific temperatures for Sieve-31B-v3. Finally, Jev-1.14 and GPT-6 Luna predict ratings on the 100-level scale through classification over probabilities rounded to two decimal places, resulting in coarser predicted ratings than those of open-weight models.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Task 2 asks models to rate the intelligence, morality, attractiveness, likability, and work ethic of residents of real places. We include these questions solely to measure social bias, following Manvi et al. (2024a), and use infant mortality only as proxy for socioeconomic conditions. We do not endorse any of the resulting ratings. All datasets are public research benchmarks used under their original licenses. We release our annotations, model predictions, and the source data whose licenses permit redistribution for non-commercial research; iNaturalist images are not redistributed and must be obtained from their original source.

sections.title: A Data Contamination
sections.content: Both source benchmarks in GEODECISIONS, LocBench (Wu et al., 2024) and the location-rating benchmark of Manvi et al. (2024a), were publicly released prior to all evaluated models, and evaluation queries sent to closed-source APIs may be retained for subsequent training (Balloccu et al., 2024). Observed accuracy or apparent fairness could therefore reflect two distinct confounders rather than genuine spatial awareness or unbiased behavior (Sainz et al., 2023): verbatim item memorization, which inflates task performance, or benchmark-specific tuning, where models are aligned to appear unbiased specifically under the published prompt template. Because none of the evaluated models disclose their training corpora, we conduct three complementary black-box diagnostics, each contrasting the published benchmark against matched control designed to reduce the risk of memorization: ❶ option-order sensitivity on Task 1, ❷ data contamination quiz on Task 2, and ❸ template rewording on Task 2. Across all three tests, we find minimal evidence of benchmark memorization or template-specific leakage, apart from small original-order gain for GPT-6 Luna. et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2024). To test for this effect on Task 1, we re-evaluate all eight models in the Image and Image + Coordinates settings on the same 2,000-sample subsets used for the closedsource models. Each subset is evaluated under three random label permutations and, for fMoW and YFCC, under the original unshuffled dataset class order. We exclude iNat2017 and iNat2018 from the original-order comparison because their candidate shortlists are ranked by the TorchSpatial image classifiers confidence, which would directly leak the ground-truth label if left unshuffled. Table 6 shows no signs of item memorization for the open-weight models. Across all 24 of their modeldatasetsetting comparisons on fMoW and YFCC, original-order top-1 accuracy differs from the shuffled mean by 0.9 to +1.3% (overall mean +0.05%, higher in only 8 of 24 cases), falling within the natural variation across random permutations (median standard deviation 0.44%). Item-level error patterns strengthen this finding: the proportion of samples answered correctly only under the original order closely matches the proportion answered correctly only across all three shuffled orders (net difference between 0.4% and +0.5%). Beyond ruling out memorization, these results indicate that decision fine-tuning substantially reduces permutation sensitivity: the open-weight decision models maintain consistent predictions on 6680% of samples, whereas the base LLMs output the same prediction across all three random orderings on 5557% of samples. This small but consistent gain may reflect exposure to the original class order, or an interaction between the fixed order and GPT-6 Lunas strong position bias (Appendix A.2). Our tests cannot distinguish the two. A.3 Template Rewording Template-based bias evaluations can be brittle to meaning-preserving edits (Seshadri et al., 2022). model aligned specifically against published benchmark would appear unbiased only under its exact template wording. This diagnostic is particularly pertinent for GPT-6 Luna, whose near-zero social bias score in Section 6.3 stems from tightly compressed ratings around 5.0. We re-evaluate both closed-source models on fixed 500-location subset of Task 2 in the Coordinates and Place Name settings across all five subjective topics and two objective controls (average temperature and infant mortality). Alongside the original template, we test four meaning-preserving variants: ❶ reworded preamble, ❷ paraphrased topic descriptions (e.g., How smart the people who live here are), ❸ coarser 15 ordinal scale, and ❹ reversed 0.09.9 scale where 0.0 denotes the highest level. Ratings are mapped back to the 0.09.9 scale for scoring. Table 8 shows that neither model exhibits weaker bias specifically under the original template. For Jev-1.14, intelligence ratings remain strongly and negatively correlated with infant mortality across every variant (ρ between 0.72 and 0.76 with Coordinates, and between 0.83 and 0.90 with Place Name). For GPT-6 Luna, intelligence ratings stay negatively correlated with infant mortality under every variant except the reversed scale with 13 place names (ρ = 0.01), and its rating compression on intelligence, morality, and attractiveness persists across templates (MAD 0.14 on all 0.0 9.9 variants. On the 15 scale, MAD 0.30 reflects quantization, as one scale step spans roughly 2.5 points after rescaling). Rather than revealing template-specific tuning, rewording primarily shifts GPT-6 Lunas refusal rate; for instance, increasing refusals on intelligence in the Coordinates setting from 10% under the original template to 61% under the reversed scale. Across variants, both models maintain strong correlations with ground truth on the objective controls (temperature ρ 0.74; infant mortality ρ 0.54), confirming that the perturbed prompts continue to elicit valid ratings. The sole exception is Jev-1.14 on infant mortality under the reversed scale (ρ = 0.17 and 0.10), where it spreads probability mass nearly uniformly instead of inverting the scale. A.4 Summary and Scope Overall, our three black-box diagnostics show little evidence of data leakage: original and shuffled label orders yield equivalent Task 1 accuracy for the open-weight models, with only small originalorder gain for GPT-6 Luna, published and neverpublished Task 2 descriptions are favored equally often, and the bias profiles of both closed-source models persist across almost all template perturbations. Nevertheless, black-box testing cannot definitively rule out every form of indirect pretraining exposure. Moreover, the contamination quiz and template rewording cover only Task 2 and the closed-source models, motivated by the fact that GPT-6 Luna is the only model with near-zero bias score and Jev-1.14 is also closed-sourced.

We port SSI and the scale-grid SRE from the GeoBS reference implementation (Wang et al., 2025b), whose code names SRE as SRI, and verify SSI against its saved outputs. We make three corrections to SRE: ❶ neighborhoods index dataset samples rather than positions within each centers nearest-neighbor list; ❷ every cells histogram uses the neighborhoods bin edges rather than bins fitted to the cells own range; and ❸ direction sectors use the initial great-circle bearing. We report SRE with the scale-grid partition. Parameters. For Task 1, SSI uses 100 km radius and 4-nearest-neighbor weight matrix, as in TorchSpatial (Wu et al., 2024), with each neighborhood capped at its 400 nearest samples and about five background points per sample, the GeoBS default. SRE follows the GeoBS example configuration, rounded to 300 km radius and 60 km cells, with two histogram bins for the binary Hit@1 marks, and cells with fewer than 20 samples are skipped. Both scores are computed around 2,000 evaluation centers per dataset, shared across models and drawn by stratified sampling on 10 grid with allocation proportional to the number of samples per cell, so they preserve the spatial distribution of the dataset.
